title: One body (1 Corinthians 12:12–27)
hook: the eye can't say to the hand I don't need you

segments.voice: Yesterday, commemoration: Paul wrote down the words of the Last Supper, the oldest written account we have. Your line was I received of the lord. What did you hand on? Day five hundred seventy-three.

Corinth had a healing shrine to the Greek god Asclepius, and people who believed they'd been cured left clay models of the part that got better: a hand, a foot, an ear, an eye. Archaeologists have dug them up there. Some scholars wonder whether Paul's readers thought of those shelves of separate clay limbs when they heard today's chapter. Because the church in Corinth was falling into pieces. People with showy gifts felt important. Quiet people felt they didn't count. Paul answers with a body, and not a pile of parts.
screen: `CLAY HANDS AND FEET IN CORINTH.` → `WHOSE GIFT MATTERS MOST?` → `PAUL ANSWERS WITH A BODY.`

segments.voice: His picture is simple enough for a child. The body has many members, and all of them together are one body. Then he gives the parts voices. The foot says: because I am not the hand, I am not of the body. Or the ear sulking because it isn't an eye. If the whole body were an eye, he asks, where would the hearing be? Then he turns to the ones who feel superior: "And the eye cannot say to the hand: I need not thy help; nor again the head to the feet: I have no need of you." In fact, he says, the members that seem weaker are necessary, and we give the less honored parts more care. If one member suffers, all suffer with it. If one is honored, all rejoice. Then the line it's all been building to: "Now you are the body of Christ, and members of member." The image wasn't new. The Roman historian Livy tells an old fable of the limbs and the belly, used to persuade the common people to go back to serving the city's rulers. Paul uses the body the other way round, to give the weaker parts more honor. Catholics read this chapter as one of the roots of a central teaching: the Church is the Mystical Body of Christ, with Christ as the head and the faithful as the members. Pope Pius the Twelfth wrote a whole encyclical on it in 1943. It's why Catholics speak of a parish in Lagos and a parish in Ohio as one body, not two clubs, and why the housebound person praying a rosary at home counts as a working member. In this body, nobody is spare.
screen: `MANY MEMBERS, ONE BODY.` · `THE EYE CAN'T SAY: I NEED NOT THY HELP.` · `THE WEAKER PARTS GET MORE HONOR.` · `THE MYSTICAL BODY OF CHRIST.` · then, large: `NOW YOU ARE THE BODY OF CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the hand you need. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone whose gift is nothing like yours. If you're a talker, a listener. If you're a planner, someone who just shows up and fixes things. Maybe someone you've quietly thought you could do without. Picture them clearly. Now notice what would fall apart if they weren't there: at work, at home, in your parish. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. Either way, decide how you'll thank them in person today, and what you'll say. The bell holds the time.
One body. Paul's picture of the Church: many members, every one of them needed, and together the body of Christ. Today's word.
Your line: the hand needs the eye. Today, thank one person whose gift is different from yours, and name the gift out loud. Day five hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Catholics speak of the Church as the Mystical Body of Christ; at Mass the bidding prayers bring the needs of the sick, the absent and the whole Church before the parish as members of one body.

fork.setup: you have a flashy gift in the Corinthian church. a quiet member asks if they even belong. what does Paul's letter tell you?
options: they belong less, but they can still come.
the parts that seem weaker are necessary.
every gift is the same, so it doesn't matter.
fork.reveal: "the eye cannot say to the hand: I need not thy help." Paul gives the weaker members more honor, not less.

original.note: Greek: body. Paul's word for the Church in 1 Corinthians 12:27, the body of Christ.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line about teamwork.
what it means: every member of the Church is needed, and the weaker ones get more honor.
what a scholar hears: Paul flips a well-worn ancient image, the body politic, which Livy's fable used to keep the lower orders serving the city's rulers.

notes: Terracotta body-part votives from the Asclepieion at Corinth: excavated in the 1930s. The link to Paul's image is a scholarly suggestion, stated as 'some scholars wonder'. Confirm.
Livy 2.32: Menenius Agrippa's fable of the belly and the limbs during the secession of the plebs. Confirm the summary.
Check Douay-Rheims wording of 12:21 and 12:27 ('members of member').
Mystici Corporis Christi, Pius XII, 29 June 1943. Confirm.
